q: A series loop contains a 20 V source, a 4.0 Ω resistor, a 5.0 Ω resistor, and a second battery V₂ opposing the first source. A meter shows the loop current is 1.0 A. Applying KVL, find V₂, in volts.
explain: KVL around the loop (20 V source taken as positive rise): 20 − (1.0)(4.0) − (1.0)(5.0) − V₂ = 0 → 20 − 4 − 5 = V₂ → V₂ = 11 V. The opposing battery 'uses up' the remaining voltage not dropped across the resistors.

q: The volt is the SI unit of electric potential difference, named after Alessandro Volta. Which ratio correctly expresses one volt?
choices: 1 J ÷ 1 C
1 J ÷ 1 A
1 C ÷ 1 J
1 A ÷ 1 Ω
explain: By definition, 1 V = 1 J/C — one joule of work done moving one coulomb of charge through the potential difference. 1 J/A = V·s (not V); 1 C/J = 1/V; 1 A/Ω = A·(A/V) = A²/V ≠ V (since Ω = V/A, so A/Ω = A²/V).

q: The schematic shows a 12 V battery driving two resistors. Find the voltage across R2.
svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 320 150" role="img" aria-label="Series circuit: 12 V battery with a 40 ohm and an 80 ohm resistor"><g stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" fill="none" stroke-linecap="round"><path d="M30 110 V40 H110 M150 40 H190 M230 40 H290 V110 H30"/><path d="M110 28 h40 v24 h-40 z"/><path d="M190 28 h40 v24 h-40 z"/><path d="M24 100 h12 M20 92 h20 M24 84 h12 M20 76 h20"/></g><g fill="currentColor" font-family="system-ui,sans-serif" font-size="13" text-anchor="middle"><text x="130" y="22">R1 = 40 Ω</text><text x="210" y="22">R2 = 80 Ω</text><text x="64" y="90">12 V</text><text x="160" y="135">series loop</text></g></svg>
caption: Two resistors in series across a 12 V source.
explain: In series the same current flows through both: I = V/(R1+R2) = 12/(40+80) = 0.1 A. Then V2 = I x R2 = 0.1 x 80 = 8 V. (Check: V1 = 0.1 x 40 = 4 V, and 4 + 8 = 12 V.)

q: Two identical positive point charges are moved from 1.0 m apart to 0.25 m apart. By what factor does the electric potential energy of the system change?
choices: It doubles
It increases by a factor of 16
It increases by a factor of 4
It decreases to one-quarter of its original value
explain: Electric potential energy between two point charges: U = kq²/r. Since U is proportional to 1/r, the ratio is U_final/U_initial = r_initial/r_final = 1.0/0.25 = 4. The energy increases by a factor of 4 because the distance decreased by a factor of 4, and work is done against the repulsive force. 'Factor of 16' is the force ratio (F ∝ 1/r²), not the energy ratio. 'Decreases' is wrong because like charges repel — bringing them closer always raises the potential energy.

q: A 120 Ω resistor is connected directly across a sinusoidal AC source whose peak voltage is 170 V. What is the average power, in watts, dissipated by the resistor?
explain: Average power in a resistive AC load requires RMS values, not peak values. Step 1 — find V_rms: V_rms = V_peak / √2 = 170 / 1.4142 ≈ 120.2 V. Step 2 — compute power: P = V_rms² / R = (170)² / (2 × 120) = 28900 / 240 ≈ 120 W. A common error is using V_peak directly, giving P = 170²/120 ≈ 241 W — exactly twice the correct answer, because P_avg = P_peak / 2 for a sine wave.

q: A copper wire has a resistance of 6.0 Ω. The wire is then drawn through a die until its length exactly doubles; its volume and resistivity remain unchanged throughout. What is the resistance of the stretched wire, in ohms?
explain: Resistance R = ρL/A. Because volume V = L·A is constant, doubling the length (L′ = 2L) forces the cross-sectional area to halve (A′ = A/2). New resistance: R′ = ρ(2L)/(A/2) = 4·(ρL/A) = 4R₀ = 4 × 6.0 = 24 Ω. A common error is concluding R only doubles because L doubled — that ignores the simultaneous halving of A that constant volume requires.

q: A GFCI outlet trips when it senses a difference greater than about 5 mA between the current in the hot conductor and the current in the neutral conductor. In which scenario would the GFCI NOT protect the person involved?
choices: A person standing on wet concrete touches the metal case of a defective power tool and current flows through their body to ground
A person simultaneously grasps the hot prong and the neutral prong of an unplugged extension cord, forming a hand-to-hand current path
A hair dryer falls into a water-filled sink, sending current from the hot wire through the water to the grounded metal drain
Damaged cord insulation allows the hot conductor to contact the grounded metal frame of an appliance
explain: The GFCI measures |I_hot − I_neutral|. In choice B current leaves through the hot prong, travels hand-to-hand through the person, and returns through the neutral prong. Both conductors carry identical current, so the difference is zero and the GFCI never trips — the person receives a shock with no protection. Choices A, C, and D all route current to ground without it returning through neutral, creating an imbalance that trips the GFCI within milliseconds.

q: Unlike most metals, the electrical resistance of a pure (intrinsic) semiconductor such as silicon DECREASES as temperature rises. Which explanation is correct?
choices: Increased atomic vibrations scatter conduction electrons more often, lowering the resistance.
The crystal lattice contracts at higher temperatures, opening wider conduction pathways.
In a semiconductor, resistance is determined solely by doping concentration and does not vary with temperature.
Thermal energy promotes more valence electrons across the band gap into the conduction band, sharply increasing the number of charge carriers.
explain: In a metal, resistance rises with temperature because lattice vibrations scatter carriers more (the carrier count barely changes). In an intrinsic semiconductor the dominant effect is carrier generation: thermal energy excites valence electrons across the band gap, so the carrier concentration rises exponentially with temperature — overwhelmingly outweighing the also-present increase in scattering — and resistance falls. Distractor A gets the scattering direction right but draws the wrong conclusion for semiconductors; more scattering alone would raise resistance, but the flood of new carriers wins. Distractor B states incorrect physics — solids thermally expand, not contract. Distractor C conflates extrinsic (doped) semiconductors with intrinsic ones; even doped semiconductors show temperature dependence, and intrinsic silicon has no intentional dopants at all.

q: The schematic shows a relay control circuit. The 15 V supply drives a series chain of Rs (unknown), an indicator LED (forward voltage 1.8 V), and a relay coil (360 Ω). The relay pulls in whenever coil current is at least 30 mA. What is the maximum Rs, in ohms, that still guarantees pull-in?
svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 170" role="img" aria-label="Relay control circuit: 15 V source, Rs, LED indicator, and 360-ohm relay coil in series"><g stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" fill="none" stroke-linecap="round"><path d="M42 55 H85"/><rect x="85" y="43" width="55" height="24"/><path d="M140 55 H172"/><path d="M172 41 L172 69 L204 55 Z"/><path d="M204 41 V69"/><path d="M204 55 H238"/><rect x="238" y="43" width="82" height="24"/><path d="M320 55 H370 V130 H42"/><path d="M42 55 V72"/><path d="M28 72 H56"/><path d="M33 80 H51"/><path d="M42 80 V130"/></g><g fill="currentColor" font-family="system-ui,sans-serif" font-size="12" text-anchor="middle"><text x="112" y="40">Rs = ?</text><text x="188" y="36">LED</text><text x="188" y="86">1.8 V</text><text x="279" y="40">Coil</text><text x="279" y="86">360 Ω</text><text x="20" y="77">15 V</text><text x="20" y="60" font-size="11">+</text><text x="20" y="128" font-size="11">−</text></g></svg>
caption: Series relay control circuit: 15 V supply, Rs, LED indicator, and 360 Ω coil.
explain: Step 1 — the LED drops 1.8 V, so the voltage shared by Rs and the coil is 15 − 1.8 = 13.2 V. Step 2 — pull-in requires I ≥ 30 mA = 0.030 A. Step 3 — maximum total resistance = V / I_min = 13.2 / 0.030 = 440 Ω. Step 4 — Rs_max = 440 − 360 = 80 Ω. Any Rs above 80 Ω starves the coil below the pull-in threshold and the relay stays open. A common error is ignoring the LED voltage drop and computing 15 / 0.030 = 500 Ω total, then Rs = 140 Ω — in real hardware that relay would fail to close because the LED eats 1.8 V of the available headroom.

q: A 5-band precision resistor has the color bands Brown–Green–Black–Red–Brown, read from the band closest to the lead. What is its resistance and tolerance?
explain: In a 5-band resistor the first three bands are significant digits, the fourth is the multiplier, and the fifth is tolerance. Brown=1, Green=5, Black=0 → significant digits 1-5-0. Red multiplier = ×10² = 100. Value: 150 × 100 = 15,000 Ω = 15 kΩ. Brown tolerance band = ±1%. Common errors: treating Black as ×1 instead of ×10⁰ gives 150 Ω (choice C); reading only the first two digit bands and treating the third as the multiplier gives 1.5 kΩ with the wrong tolerance (choice A); confusing the Brown tolerance band for Gold (±5%) gives choice D.

q: A full-wave bridge rectifier is built from four silicon diodes, each with a 0.7 V forward drop. The transformer secondary delivers 15 V RMS. What is the peak value of the rectified output voltage, in volts?
explain: Step 1 — convert secondary RMS to peak: V_peak = V_rms × √2 = 15 × 1.4142 = 21.21 V. Step 2 — in a bridge rectifier two diodes conduct on each half-cycle (one on the positive path in, one on the return path), so the total forward-voltage penalty is 2 × 0.7 = 1.4 V. Step 3 — peak output: V_out = 21.21 − 1.4 = 19.81 V ≈ 19.8 V. A common error is subtracting only one diode drop (giving 20.5 V) because students forget that current passes through two diodes per half-cycle in a bridge. A second error is using V_rms directly without converting to peak, giving 15 − 1.4 = 13.6 V.

q: Three 2-input NAND gates implement a logic function from inputs A and B. Gate 1 has both its inputs tied to A; Gate 2 has both its inputs tied to B; Gate 3 takes Gate 1's output and Gate 2's output as its two inputs. Which function does the output Z compute?
choices: A AND B — because stacking three NAND gates cancels two inversions and restores the AND function
NOT A — because the first NAND gate dominates the network and suppresses the B path
A OR B — because NOT(NOT A · NOT B) equals A + B by De Morgan's theorem
A XOR B — because having separate single-input inversion paths produces the exclusive difference
explain: Gate 1: NAND(A, A) = NOT(A·A) = NOT A. Gate 2: NAND(B, B) = NOT(B·B) = NOT B. Gate 3: NAND(NOT A, NOT B) = NOT(NOT A · NOT B). Apply De Morgan's law: NOT(NOT A · NOT B) = NOT(NOT A) + NOT(NOT B) = A + B = A OR B. This is the classic 3-NAND implementation of OR — a direct consequence of NAND being a universal gate. Distractor A: for A=1, B=0, Gate 1→0, Gate 2→1, Gate 3=NAND(0,1)=1, but A AND B=0 — wrong. Distractor B ignores Gate 2 entirely. Distractor D: for A=1, B=1, the network outputs NAND(0,0)=1, but A XOR B=0 — wrong.

q: The schematic shows a two-mesh ladder circuit driven by a single 18 V source. Mesh currents I₁ (left mesh) and I₂ (right mesh) are both defined clockwise. Find the magnitude of the current, in amperes, flowing through the shared 6 Ω resistor.
svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 360 200" role="img" aria-label="Two-mesh ladder circuit: 18 V source left, 3 ohm top, shared 6 ohm middle, 2 ohm right"><g stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" fill="none" stroke-linecap="round"><line x1="50" y1="50" x2="50" y2="86"/><line x1="36" y1="86" x2="64" y2="86"/><line x1="42" y1="98" x2="58" y2="98"/><line x1="50" y1="98" x2="50" y2="160"/><line x1="50" y1="50" x2="80" y2="50"/><rect x="80" y="42" width="65" height="16"/><line x1="145" y1="50" x2="180" y2="50"/><line x1="180" y1="50" x2="310" y2="50"/><line x1="180" y1="50" x2="180" y2="76"/><rect x="172" y="76" width="16" height="52"/><line x1="180" y1="128" x2="180" y2="160"/><line x1="310" y1="50" x2="310" y2="76"/><rect x="302" y="76" width="16" height="52"/><line x1="310" y1="128" x2="310" y2="160"/><line x1="50" y1="160" x2="310" y2="160"/></g><g fill="currentColor" font-family="system-ui,sans-serif" font-size="13" text-anchor="middle"><text x="112" y="38">3 Ω</text><text x="197" y="105">6 Ω</text><text x="330" y="105">2 Ω</text><text x="27" y="90">+</text><text x="27" y="102">−</text><text x="27" y="118">18 V</text><text x="112" y="125">I₁</text><text x="245" y="125">I₂</text></g></svg>
caption: Ladder circuit: 18 V source, 3 Ω series branch, shared 6 Ω centre leg, 2 Ω terminating branch. Both mesh currents clockwise.
explain: Write mesh equations (self-resistance × own current minus shared resistance × other current = net source voltage). Mesh 1: (3+6)I₁ − 6I₂ = 18 → 9I₁ − 6I₂ = 18. Mesh 2: (6+2)I₂ − 6I₁ = 0 → −6I₁ + 8I₂ = 0. From equation 2: I₁ = (4/3)I₂. Substitute into equation 1: 9·(4/3)I₂ − 6I₂ = 12I₂ − 6I₂ = 6I₂ = 18, so I₂ = 3 A and I₁ = 4 A. The shared 6 Ω carries the difference of the two mesh currents: |I₁ − I₂| = |4 − 3| = 1 A. Verification — Mesh 1: 18 − 3(4) − 6(1) = 0 ✓; Mesh 2: 6(1) − 2(3) = 0 ✓. A common error is treating the two meshes as independent, applying Ohm's law to the 6 Ω without the opposing I₂ contribution, which incorrectly gives 18/9 = 2 A.

q: Gustav Kirchhoff is best known in circuit lab for his two circuit laws, but he also made a landmark contribution to science by collaborating with Robert Bunsen at Heidelberg University. What did their joint work establish?
choices: That blackbody radiation is emitted in discrete packets — a discovery that launched quantum mechanics
That every chemical element emits and absorbs light at a unique set of wavelengths, enabling identification of elements in distant stars
That the force between magnetic poles obeys the same inverse-square law as Coulomb's force between electric charges
That electromagnetic waves travel at the speed of light, confirming Maxwell's wave theory
explain: Kirchhoff and Bunsen developed spectral analysis (spectroscopy) at Heidelberg in the late 1850s–1860s. They showed that each element has a characteristic line spectrum and used this to identify sodium in the solar spectrum by matching solar absorption lines against lab emission lines — the first remote chemical analysis of a star. Choice A is Planck's 1900 quantum theory (Kirchhoff did formulate a law of thermal radiation, but the quantum step was Planck's, not a Kirchhoff–Bunsen result). Choice C is an inverse-square magnetic law explored by Coulomb and others, unrelated to the Kirchhoff–Bunsen collaboration. Choice D summarises Hertz's 1887 radio-wave experiments.

q: Three point charges sit on the x-axis: q₁ = +3.0 μC at x = 0, q₂ = −1.0 μC at x = 0.20 m, and q₃ = +2.0 μC at x = 0.40 m. Using k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N·m²/C², find the magnitude of the net electrostatic force on q₂, in newtons.
svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 420 100" role="img" aria-label="Three collinear point charges"><g stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" fill="none" stroke-linecap="round"><line x1="20" y1="52" x2="395" y2="52"/><polyline points="388,47 395,52 388,57"/><circle cx="60" cy="52" r="12"/><circle cx="210" cy="52" r="12"/><circle cx="360" cy="52" r="12"/></g><g fill="currentColor" font-family="system-ui,sans-serif" text-anchor="middle" font-size="12"><text x="60" y="14">q₁ = +3.0 μC</text><text x="210" y="14">q₂ = −1.0 μC</text><text x="360" y="14">q₃ = +2.0 μC</text><text x="60" y="78">x = 0</text><text x="210" y="78">x = 0.20 m</text><text x="360" y="78">x = 0.40 m</text><text x="400" y="55" text-anchor="start">x</text></g></svg>
caption: Three collinear point charges spaced 0.20 m apart.
explain: Step 1 — force directions on q₂. q₁ (+) and q₂ (−) attract, pulling q₂ toward −x; q₃ (+) and q₂ (−) attract, pulling q₂ toward +x. The two forces oppose each other. Step 2 — Coulomb magnitudes (both pairs share r = 0.20 m): F₁₂ = (8.99×10⁹)(3.0×10⁻⁶)(1.0×10⁻⁶)/(0.20)² = 0.6743 N; F₃₂ = (8.99×10⁹)(2.0×10⁻⁶)(1.0×10⁻⁶)/(0.20)² = 0.4495 N. Step 3 — net magnitude: |0.6743 − 0.4495| = 0.2248 N ≈ 0.225 N (net toward q₁). Common error: adding both forces instead of subtracting opposing contributions, giving 1.12 N — more than four times too large.

q: The full-cycle average of a pure sinusoidal AC voltage is zero. Why does a resistor connected to this source still dissipate power continuously?
choices: Current in a pure resistor leads voltage by 90°, so when voltage is zero, current is at its peak; the product v·i is therefore always positive and averages to a nonzero value.

Power equals v²/R; since v² = V²_peak·sin²(ωt) is always non-negative, its cycle average is V²_peak/2 — exactly what V_RMS captures: V_RMS = V_peak/√2. Average power P = V²_RMS/R is therefore nonzero even though v averages to zero.

The resistor dissipates energy only during the positive half-cycle; during the negative half-cycle no power is dissipated, so the cycle average equals half the positive-half-cycle average — still nonzero.
The full-cycle average of AC voltage is not zero; a true AC voltmeter reads the RMS value V_peak/√2, which is the genuine cycle average.
explain: Power in a resistor at every instant is p(t) = v(t)²/R = V²_peak·sin²(ωt)/R. Because v² ≥ 0 always, p(t) ≥ 0 always — the resistor converts electrical energy to heat in BOTH half-cycles, never reversing. The cycle average of sin²(ωt) is 1/2, giving P_avg = V²_peak/(2R) = V²_RMS/R, where V_RMS ≡ V_peak/√2. The key point: average(v²) ≠ [average(v)]² — squaring and averaging are not interchangeable. Choice A is wrong: in a pure resistor V and I are exactly IN phase (0° shift), not 90° — a 90° phase lead belongs to capacitors. Choice C is wrong: the negative half-cycle also produces positive power (p = v²/R ≥ 0 whether v is positive or negative). Choice D is wrong: the arithmetic cycle average of a sine wave IS zero; V_RMS is the root-mean-SQUARE, not the arithmetic mean.

q: A light bulb is rated 60 W at 120 V RMS and behaves as a pure resistor at its operating temperature. It is connected to a standard 120 V RMS sinusoidal AC outlet. What is the peak instantaneous power, in watts, dissipated by the bulb at the moment the voltage reaches its positive maximum?
explain: Step 1 — find bulb resistance from the rating: R = V²_RMS / P_avg = (120)² / 60 = 14 400 / 60 = 240 Ω. Step 2 — find peak voltage: V_peak = V_RMS × √2 = 120 × 1.4142 ≈ 169.7 V. Step 3 — peak instantaneous power: P_peak = V²_peak / R = (169.7)² / 240 = 28 800 / 240 = 120 W. Shortcut: P_peak = (√2 × V_RMS)² / R = 2 × V²_RMS / R = 2 × P_avg = 2 × 60 = 120 W. For any resistor on sinusoidal AC, peak instantaneous power is always exactly twice the average power. Common error: substituting V_RMS directly into P = V²/R gives 60 W — that is the rated average, not the peak; the √2 step from RMS to peak must not be skipped.
